label: lem:weak-topology
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:weak-topology}
Let $(H,\tau)$ be a semitopological group whose continuous real-valued
functions separate points. Let $\tau_c$ be the initial topology on $H$
generated by $C((H,\tau),\mathbb{R})$. Then $(H,\tau_c)$ is the Tychonoff reflection
of $(H,\tau)$, with the identity as its canonical homomorphism. It is
quasitopological whenever $(H,\tau)$ is quasitopological. If $H$ is
Lindel\"of, $(H,\tau_c)$ is also its regular reflection.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $C((H,\tau),\mathbb{R})$ denote the set of all continuous real-valued functions on $(H, \tau)$. Consider the evaluation map
$$
e: H \to \mathbb{R}^{C((H,\tau),\mathbb{R})},
$$
defined by $e(x) = (f(x))_{f \in C((H,\tau),\mathbb{R})}$ for each $x\in H$.
Since the continuous real-valued functions $C((H,\tau),\mathbb{R})$ separate points, the map $e$ is injective. The initial topology on $H$ generated by $C((H,\tau),\mathbb{R})$ is denoted by $\tau_c$. Then one can easily show that $
e: (H,\tau_c)\to \mathbb{R}^{C((H,\tau),\mathbb{R})}$ is a topological embedding, which implies that $(H, \tau_c)$ is a Tychonoff space and $\tau_c\subseteq \tau$.

Next, we show that $(H, \tau_c)$ is a semitopological group. Let $L_g: H \to H$ denote the left translations by $g \in H$. Take any subbasic element $f^{-1}(U)$ in $(H,\tau_c)$, where $f\in C((H,\tau),\mathbb{R}) $ and $U$ is open in $\mathbb{R}$.
Then $L_g^{-1}(f^{-1}(U))=(f\circ L_g)^{-1}(U)$. Since $(H,\tau)$ is semitopological group, $f\circ L_g$ is a continuous function on $(H,\tau)$. Thus, $(f\circ L_g)^{-1}(U)$ is open in $(H, \tau_c)$, because $(H, \tau_c)$ is generated by $C((H,\tau),\mathbb{R})$. This shows that $L_g$ is continuous on $(H, \tau_c)$. Similarly, one can show that every right translations $R_g$ by $g \in H$ is continuous on $(H, \tau_c)$. Thus, $(H, \tau_c)$ is a semitopological group. If inversion is
$\tau$-continuous, then one can show that inversion is
$\tau_c$-continuous by the same way.

Now we verify the universal property for the Tychonoff reflection. Let $f:(H,\tau)\to X$ be continuous, where $X$ is Tychonoff. Embed
$X$ into a product of real lines, say $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^I$ for some index set $I$. For each coordinate projection $\pi_\alpha: \mathbb{R}^I \to \mathbb{R}$, the composition $\pi_\alpha \circ f$ is a continuous real-valued function on $(H, \tau)$, hence $\pi_\alpha \circ f \in C((H,\tau),\mathbb{R})$. By the definition of $\tau_c$, each $\pi_\alpha \circ f$ is continuous with respect to $\tau_c$. The identity map $id_H: (H, \tau) \to (H, \tau_c)$ is continuous because $\tau_c \subseteq \tau$, and we have $f = f \circ id_H$. This proves that $(H, \tau_c)$ is the Tychonoff reflection of $(H, \tau)$.

Finally, suppose $H$ is Lindel\"of. Let $X$ be a regular space and $f: (H, \tau) \to X$ a continuous map. The subspace $f(H)$ is
Lindel\"of and regular and hence is normal, so $f(H)$
is Tychonoff. Applying the Tychonoff reflection property to the corestriction $f: (H, \tau) \to f(H)$, we obtain a continuous map $h: (H, \tau_c) \to f(H)$ such that $f = h \circ id_H$. Therefore, $(H, \tau_c)$ is also the regular reflection of $(H, \tau)$.

label: lem:semiregular
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:semiregular}
The quasitopological group $G$ defined by (\ref{eq:cones2}) is countable, second-countable, Hausdorff and semiregular but is not regular.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$G$ is first-countable and countable, $G$ is second-countable. Since the topology $\tau$ of $G$ is finer than the Euclidean subspace topology $\rho$, $G$ is Hausdorff and
\[
 \operatorname{cl}_\tau U_n\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_\rho U_n
 =\{(s,t)\in E:|t|\leq |s|\leq1/n\}=:K_n.
\]
A point of $K_n\setminus U_n$ has nonzero first coordinate. If
$|s|=1/n$, arbitrarily small horizontal displacements away from the
vertical axis leave $K_n$. If $|t|=|s|<1/n$, horizontal displacements
toward that axis leave $K_n$. Such displacements belong to every
sufficiently large $U_m$. Hence $\operatorname{Int}_\tau K_n=U_n$, and $U_n$ is
regular open. Translates give semiregularity.

By~\eqref{eq:boundary}, the closure of every $U_n$ contains a point
$(r,r)\ne o$, which is outside $U_1$. Thus no neighborhood of $o$ has
closure contained in $U_1$, and $G$ is not regular.
head: environment

label: lem:new-closure
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:new-closure}
The point $o$ belongs to $\operatorname{cl}_Y A$, where $A$ and $Y$ are defined by (\ref{eq:K-A}) and (\ref{eq:Y-E}), respectively.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $O$ be an open neighborhood of $o$ in $Y$. By regularity, choose
an open neighborhood $V$ of $o$ such that $\operatorname{cl}_Y V\subseteq O$.
Since $q$ is continuous, some $U_n$ is contained in $V$. Continuity
also gives
\[
       \operatorname{cl}_\tau U_n\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_Y U_n
                     \subseteq\operatorname{cl}_Y V\subseteq O.
\]
Choose a rational $r$ with $0<r<1/n$. By~\eqref{eq:boundary}, the
point $z=(r,r)$ belongs to $O$. The set $O$ is $\tau$-open, so
$z+U_m\subseteq O$ for some $m$. Take a rational $d$ with
$0<d<\min\{r,1/m\}$. Then
\[
       a=(r-d,r)=z+(-d,0)\in O\cap A.
\]
Every neighborhood $O$ therefore meets $A$.
head: environment

label: lem:bump
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:bump}
Suppose $(a_j)_{j\geq1}$ is a sequence in $A$ defined by (\ref{eq:K-A}) such that
\[
 0<\|a_{j+1}\|<\tfrac14\|a_j\|\quad(j\geq1).
\]
There exists a continuous function $f:G\to[0,1]$ such that $f|_K=0$ and
$f(a_j)=1$ for every $j\geq1$, where $G$ and $K$ are defined by (\ref{eq:cones2}) and (\ref{eq:K-A}), respectively.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $A$ is open in $E$ with Euclidean topology $\rho$, for each $a_j$ we can choose $r_j>0$ so that the Euclidean ball $B_{r_j}^{a_j}=\{x\in E:\|x-a_j\|<r_j \}$ is contained in $A$ and $r_j<\|a_j\|/4$.
Since
\begin{align*}
3\|a_j\|/4 &= \bigl| \|a_j\|/4 - \|a_j\| \bigr| \\
           &< \bigl| \|x-a_j\| - \|a_j\| \bigr| \\
           &\leq \|x\| \\
           &\leq \|x-a_j\| + \|a_j\| \\
           &< \|a_j\|/4 + \|a_j\| \\
           &= 5\|a_j\|/4,
\end{align*}
 the balls $\{B_{r_j}^{a_j}:j\geq 1\}$ are pairwise
disjoint and they form a locally finite family in $(E\setminus\{o\},\rho)$.
For each $j\geq 1$, define $b_j:E\setminus\{o\}\to [0,1]$ by
$$
 b_j(x)=\max\{0,1-\|x-a_j\|/r_j\},
$$
 for each $x\in E\setminus\{o\}.$ Clear, the family $\{b_j: j\geq 1\}$ of continuous functions is locally finite, so $f:E\to [0,1]$ defined by
 $$f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty b_j(x)$$
 for each $x\in E\setminus\{o\}$ and $f(o)=0$ is $\rho$-continuous at each point $x\in E\setminus\{o\}$ and hence $f$ is $\tau$-continuous at each point $x\in E\setminus\{o\}$ by $\rho\subseteq \tau$.
 $f$ vanishes on $K$ defined by (\ref{eq:K-A}), and in particular on the $\tau$-neighborhood
$U_1$ of $o$, so it is also $\tau$-continuous at $o$. Thus $f:G\to[0,1]$ is continuous. Finally,
$f(a_j)=1$ for every $j\geq1$ and $f|_K=0$ by construction.
head: environment

label: prop:not-frechet
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{lem:new-closure}, the point $o$ belongs to $\operatorname{cl}_Y A$, where $A$ is defined by (\ref{eq:K-A}). Suppose a sequence in $A$ converges to $o$ in $Y$. By
\eqref{eq:topology-order}, it also converges to $o$ in the Euclidean
topology. It therefore has a subsequence $(a_j)$ satisfying the
hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:bump}. Let $f$ be the function provided
by that lemma. The definition of $\tau_c$ makes $f$ continuous on
$Y$, so convergence would imply $f(a_j)\to f(o)=0$. This contradicts
$f(a_j)=1$. Thus, we have proved that $Y$ is not a
Fr\'echet--Urysohn space.
head: environment

label: thm:main-example
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $G$ be defined by (\ref{eq:cones2}). Then $G$ is a countable, second-countable, Hausdorff, semiregular
quasitopological abelian group by Lemma \ref{lem:semiregular}. Since the topology $\tau$ of $G$ is finer than the Euclidean subspace topology $\rho$, continuous real-valued
functions on $G$ separate points.

 By Lemma \ref{lem:weak-topology}, $Y=(E,\tau_c)$ defined by (\ref{eq:Y-E}) is the $\operatorname{Tych}(G)$ and $\operatorname{Reg}(G)$. Clearly, the canonical maps to $\operatorname{Reg}(G)$ and $\operatorname{Tych}(G)$ are bijective. Thus,
(i) and (ii) are proved.

For (iii). From Proposition \ref{prop:not-frechet} and (ii) it follows that $\operatorname{Reg}(G)$ and $\operatorname{Tych}(G)$ are not Fr\'echet--Urysohn.
 Since every countable Tychonoff space is zero-dimensional, $\operatorname{Tych}(G)$ is zero-dimensional Hence, so is $\operatorname{Reg}(G)$ by (ii).
head: environment

label: rem:boundary-sequence
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:boundary-sequence}
The boundary sequence $z_j=(1/j,1/j)$ does converge to $o$ in $Y$.
Indeed, the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:new-closure} shows that every
$Y$-neighborhood of $o$ contains $\operatorname{cl}_\tau U_n$ for some $n$, and
\eqref{eq:boundary} contains the tail of $(z_j)$ in this closure.
In $G$ the same sequence never enters $U_1$. The obstruction in
Proposition~\ref{prop:not-frechet} is different: points strictly
outside $K$ cannot approach $o$ by any sequence in the reflected topology.
head: environment

label: lem:d-open
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:d-open}
Let $p:X\to Z$ be a continuous $d$-open surjection, with $Z$ regular.
For $x\in X$,
\[
                   \chi(p(x),Z)\leq\chi(x,X).
\]
Also $w(Z)\leq w(X)$, with cardinal invariants taken to be infinite.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a local base $\mathcal B$ of open neighborhoods of $x$, put
$V_B=\operatorname{Int}_Z\operatorname{cl}_Z p(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal B$. These sets contain
$p(x)$ by $d$-openness. Given a neighborhood $O$ of $p(x)$, choose
an open $W$ with $p(x)\in W\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_Z W\subseteq O$, and then
$B\in\mathcal B$ with $B\subseteq p^{-1}(W)$. It follows that
$V_B\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_Z W\subseteq O$, proving the character bound.
The same argument, using a base for $X$ and choosing a preimage of
each point of $Z$, proves the weight bound.
head: environment

label: cor:nonquotient
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A bijective quotient map is a homeomorphism, whereas $G$ is
second-countable and $Y$ is not first-countable. An open continuous
surjection is quotient. Finally, $d$-openness would contradict
Lemma~\ref{lem:d-open}.
head: environment

label: rem:semireg-reflection
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:semireg-reflection}
The example explicitly separates semiregularization from regular
reflection: $G_{\mathrm{sr}}=G$, but $G$ is not regular. Thus one cannot
identify $T_3(H)$ with $H_{\mathrm{sr}}$ for arbitrary semitopological,
or even quasitopological, groups, where $T_3$ denotes point--closed-set
separation. In particular, this identification, used in the
semitopological part of the proof of~\cite[Theorem~4.2]{PW}, does not
justify the countability assertion made there.
head: environment

label: lem:parameter-extension
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:parameter-extension}
Let $X$ be any topological space, $B$ a metrizable space, and $P$ a
nonempty closed subspace of $B$. Every continuous function
$E:X\times P\to[0,1]$ extends to a continuous function
$F:X\times B\to[0,1]$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a compatible metric $d$ on $B$. If $P=B$, there is nothing to
prove. For $b\in B\setminus P$, put $d_b=d(b,P)>0$. By
paracompactness of the metrizable space $B\setminus P$, choose a
locally finite partition of unity $(\lambda_i)_{i\in I}$ subordinate
to an open refinement of the cover
\[
       \{B_d(b,\frac{d_b}{4}):b\in B\setminus P\}.
\]
For each $i$, choose $b_i\in B\setminus P$ so that
$\{b:\lambda_i(b)>0\}\subseteq B_d(b_i,\frac{d_{b_i}}{4})$, and choose
$p_i\in P$ with $d(b_i,p_i)<2d_{b_i}$. Define $F:X\times B\to \mathbb{R}$ by
\[
 F(x,b)=
 \begin{cases}
 E(x,b),&b\in P,\\
 \displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i(b)E(x,p_i),&b\notin P
 \end{cases}
\]
for each $(x,b)\in X\times B.$

Since $(\lambda_i)_{i \in I}$ is a partition of unity, for every $b \in B \setminus P$, we have $\lambda_i(b) \ge 0$ for all $i \in I$ and $\sum_{i \in I} \lambda_i(b) = 1$. Also, since $E: X \times P \to [0,1]$, we have $E(x, p_i) \in [0,1]$ for all $x \in X$ and $p_i \in P$. Therefore, for $b \notin P$,
\[
 0 \le F(x,b) = \sum_{i \in I} \lambda_i(b) E(x, p_i) \le \sum_{i \in I} \lambda_i(b) \cdot 1 = 1.
\]
Thus, $F(x,b) \in [0,1]$ for all $(x,b) \in X \times (B \setminus P)$.

Fix an arbitrary point $(x_0, b_0) \in X \times (B \setminus P)$. Since $P$ is closed in $B$ and by the local finiteness of the partition of unity $(\lambda_i)_{i \in I}$, there exists an open neighborhood $V$ of $b_0$ contained in $B \setminus P$ such that only finitely many indices $i \in I_0 = \{i_1, \dots, i_n\}\subseteq I$ satisfy $\lambda_i|_V \neq 0$.

For any $(x,b) \in X \times V$, the defining sum reduces to a finite sum:
\[
 F(x,b) = \sum_{i \in I_0} \lambda_i(b) E(x, p_i).
\]
For each $i \in I_0$, the function $b \mapsto \lambda_i(b)$ is continuous on $B \setminus P$. Also, because $E$ is jointly continuous on $X \times P$ and $p_i \in P$ is fixed, the function $x \mapsto E(x, p_i)$ is continuous on $X$. Consequently, each term $\lambda_i(b) E(x, p_i)$ is jointly continuous on $X \times V$. Since $I_0$ is finite, the finite sum $F(x,b)$ is jointly continuous at $(x_0, b_0)$. As $(x_0, b_0)$ was arbitrary, $F$ is jointly continuous on $X \times (B \setminus P)$. Thus, $F$ is continuous at each point $(x_0, b_0) \in X \times (B \setminus P)$, because  $X \times (B \setminus P)$ is open in $X\times B$.

Fix $(x_0,p_0)\in X\times P$ and $\varepsilon>0$.
Continuity of $E$
provides a neighborhood $U$ of $x_0$ and $\delta>0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:d}
 |E(x,p)-E(x_0,p_0)|<\varepsilon
 \quad \text{for all } (x,p) \in U \times V,
\end{equation}\label{eq:Y}
where $V=\{b\in P: d(b,p_0)<\delta\}$
We have the following claim

\medskip
{\bf Claim:} $|F(x,b) - F(x_0, p_0)| < \epsilon$ whenever $(x,b) \in U \times V'$, where $V'=\{b\in B: d(b,p_0)<\delta/4\}$.
\medskip

\noindent \textit{Proof of Claim.} Take any \((x,b)\in U \times V'\). If \(b \in P\), then \(b \in V\) and the inequality follows directly from \eqref{eq:d}. Now suppose $b\notin P$ and $\lambda_i(b)>0$ for some $i\in I$. Then $d(b,b_i)<\frac{d_{b_i}}{4}$ and $$d(b,P)\geq d(b_i,P)-d(b,b_i)>d_{b_i}-\frac{d_{b_i}}{4}=\tfrac34d_{b_i}$$
and
 $$d(b,p_i)\leq d(b,b_i)+d(b_i,p_i)<\frac{d_{b_i}}{4}+2d_{b_i} =\tfrac94d_{b_i}<3d(b,P).$$
Since $p_0\in P$, we have $d(b,P)\leq d(b,p_0)$.
Thus, by $d(b,p_0)<\frac{\delta}{4}$,
$$d(p_i,p_0)\leq d(p_i,b)+d(b,p_0)<3d(b,P)+d(b,p_0)\leq4d(b,p_0)<\delta.$$
Therefore, $|E(x, p_i) - E(x_0, p_0)|<\varepsilon$ by (\ref{eq:d}) and hence,
\begin{align*}
|F(x, b) - E(x_0, p_0)| &= \left| \sum_{i \in I} \lambda_i(b) (E(x, p_i) - E(x_0, p_0)) \right|\\
& \le \sum_{i \in I} \lambda_i(b) |E(x, p_i) - E(x_0, p_0)| \\
&< \sum_{i \in I} \lambda_i(b) \varepsilon = \varepsilon.
\end{align*}
This proves the Claim. Since \((x_0,p_0)\in X\times P\) was arbitrary, \(F\) is continuous at each point of \(X\times P\). Combined with the continuity on \(X\times(B\setminus P)\), we conclude that \(F\) is continuous on \(X\times B\).
head: environment

label: lem:universal-function
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:closed-parameters
title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a countable open local base $(U_n(x))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ at each
$x\in X$. Inside the Polish group $B$ in the statement, consider
\begin{equation}\label{eq:closed-parameters}
 \begin{split}
 P=\bigl\{(v,m)\in[0,1]^X\times\mathbb{N}^{X\times\mathbb{N}}:\quad
 &|v(y)-v(x)|\leq 2^{-k}\\[-2pt]
 &\text{for all }x\in X,\ k\in\mathbb{N},\ y\in U_{m(x,k)}(x)\bigr\}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Now we shall prove that $P$ is closed in $B=\mathbb{R}^X\times\mathbb Z^{X\times\mathbb{N}}$. Let $(v_0,m_0) \in P^c= B \setminus P$. First, if $(v_0,m_0) \notin [0,1]^X \times \mathbb{N}^{X \times \mathbb{N}}$, then it can be separated from $P$ by an obvious basic open set. Thus, we may assume without loss of generality that $(v_0,m_0) \in [0,1]^X \times \mathbb{N}^{X \times \mathbb{N}}$. Since $(v_0,m_0) \notin P$, the defining inequality must fail. Hence, there exist $x_0 \in X$, $k_0 \in \mathbb{N}$, and $y_0 \in X$ such that $y_0 \in U_{m_0(x_0,k_0)}(x_0)$ and
$$
|v_0(y_0) - v_0(x_0)| > 2^{-k_0}.
$$

Set $n_0 = m_0(x_0,k_0) \in \mathbb{N}$. Define the sets $W_1, W_2 \subseteq B$ as follows:
\[
W_1 = \bigl\{(v', m') \in B : m'(x_0,k_0) = n_0\bigr\}=\pi_{x_0,k_0}^{-1}(n_0),
\]
where $\pi_{x_0,k_0} : B \to \mathbb{Z}$ is the projection map, defined by $\pi_{x_0,k_0}(v', m') = m'(x_0,k_0)$.
\[
W_2 = \bigl\{(v', m') \in B : |v'(y_0) - v'(x_0)| > 2^{-k_0}\bigr\}.
\]
Let $W = W_1 \cap W_2$. Clearly, $(v_0,m_0) \in W$.

We claim that $W$ is open in $B$. Since $\{n_0\}$ is open in $\mathbb{Z}$ and the  projection map $\pi_{x_0,k_0}$ is continuous, $W_1$ is open in $B$. For $W_2$: Consider the evaluation map $\phi : B \to \mathbb{R}^2$ defined by $\phi(v', m') = (v'(y_0), v'(x_0))$. Let $\pi_i:\mathbb{R}^2\to \mathbb{R}$ be the $i$-th projection ($i=1,2$) and $\pi_{x}:B\to \mathbb{R}$ be the $x$-th projection ($x=y_0,x_0$). Then one can easily show that $\pi_1\circ \phi = \pi_{y_0}$, $\pi_2\circ \phi = \pi_{x_0}$. Since $\pi_{y_0}$ and $\pi_{x_0}$ are continuous, $\phi$ is continuous. The set $O = \{(a,b) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |a - b| > 2^{-k_0}\}$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Therefore, $W_2 = \phi^{-1}(O)$ is open in $B$.
Thus, $W=W_1 \cap W_2$ is open in $B$.

Finally, for any $(v', m') \in W$, we have $m'(x_0,k_0) = n_0$, $y_0 \in U_{n_0}(x_0) = U_{m'(x_0,k_0)}(x_0)$, and $|v'(y_0) - v'(x_0)| > 2^{-k_0}$. This means that $(v', m')$ violates the defining condition of $P$, so $(v', m') \in P^c$. Hence, $W \subseteq P^c$, which means $P^c$ is open. Consequently, $P$ is closed in $B$.

$P$ is nonempty, as witnessed by any constant $v$.

 Define the evaluation function $$E:X\times P\longrightarrow[0,1]$$ by
$E(x,(v,m))=v(x)$ for each $(x,(v,m))\in X\times P$.

To prove $E$ is continuous, consider the map $\Phi: X \times P \to X \times [0,1]^X$ defined by $\Phi(x,(v,m)) = (x,v)$. Since the projections $\pi_X(x,(v,m))=x$ and $\pi_P(x,(v,m))=v$ are continuous, so is $\Phi$. Let $\operatorname{ev}: X \times [0,1]^X \to [0,1]$ be the evaluation map $\operatorname{ev}(x,v)=v(x)$. By the definition of the product topology on $[0,1]^X$, the evaluation map $\operatorname{ev}$ is continuous. Since $E = \operatorname{ev} \circ \Phi$, it follows that $E$ is continuous.

Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:parameter-extension} to extend $E$ to
$F:X\times B\to[0,1]$. Every member of $C(X,[0,1])$ already
occurs as a slice with parameter in $P$, and every slice of $F$
is continuous. This proves~\eqref{eq:all-slices}.
head: environment

label: lem:initiality-test
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:initiality-test}
Let $Y$ be Tychonoff and $a:Y\to L$ continuous, where $L$ is any
topological space. If every $\varphi\in C(Y,[0,1])$ has the form
$\varphi=u_\varphi\circ a$ for some $u_\varphi\in C(L,[0,1])$,
then $a$ is a topological embedding.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Continuous $[0,1]$-valued functions separate points of $Y$, so $a$
is injective. They also generate the topology of $Y$. Since each
of them is pulled back from a continuous function on $L$, the
topology induced by $a$ contains the topology of $Y$. Continuity
of $a$ gives the reverse inclusion.
head: environment

label: thm:amplification
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:amplification}
Let $G_0$ be a countable first-countable semitopological group whose
continuous real-valued functions separate points, and suppose that
$Y_0=\operatorname{Tych}(G_0)$ is not first-countable. Let $B$ and $F$ be provided
by Lemma~\ref{lem:universal-function} for the underlying space of
$G_0$, and put $H=G_0\times B$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $H$ is second-countable, and its regular and Tychonoff
reflections coincide with a Tychonoff semitopological group $Z$
having a countable network. The canonical map $r:H\to Z$ is
bijective.
\item $F$ cannot be written as $h\circ p$, with $p:H\to L$ a
continuous homomorphism to a regular first-countable semitopological
group and $h\in C(L,[0,1])$.
\item Writing $F=\bar F\circ r$, the function $\bar F$ cannot be
written as $h\circ p$ with $p:Z\to L$ a continuous homomorphism
to any first-countable semitopological group and $h\in C(L,[0,1])$.
\end{enumerate}
If $G_0$ is quasitopological or abelian, then so are $H$ and $Z$.
If $G_0$ is semiregular, then so is $H$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A countable space with countable local bases has a countable base.
Thus $H$ is second-countable and Lindel\"of. Its continuous real-valued
functions separate points, using those on $G_0$ and $B$ separately.
From Lemma~\ref{lem:weak-topology} it follows that the regular and Tychonoff
reflections of $H$ coincide, denote by $Z$, with the
initial topology generated by $C(H,\mathbb{R})$ on the same underlying
group. The images under $r$ of a countable base of $H$ form a
network for $Z$. This proves~\textup{(i)}. Let $q:G_0\to Y_0$ be
the canonical map; by the same lemma it is bijective and $Y_0$
is also $\operatorname{Reg}(G_0)$.

For~\textup{(ii)}, suppose $F=h\circ p$ as stated and write $e$
for the identity of $G_0$ and $0$ for that of $B$. Since $p:G_0\times B\rightarrow L$ is continuous, we can define a continuous
map $p_0:G_0\rightarrow L$ by $p_0(x)= p(x,0)$ for each $x\in G_0$. By the
universal property of $q$, it has the form $a\circ q$ for a
continuous map $a:Y_0\to L$. For every
$\varphi\in C(Y_0,[0,1])$, we have $\varphi\circ q \in C(G_0,[0,1])$. Hence,  by~\eqref{eq:all-slices}, we can choose $b_\varphi\in B$ such that
\[
       F(x,b_\varphi)=\varphi(q(x))
\]
holds for each $x\in G_0$. Put
$c_\varphi=p(e,b_\varphi)$. Since $F=h\circ p$ and $p$ is a homomorphism, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\varphi(q(x))&=F(x,b_\varphi)\\
  & =h\bigl(p((x,0)(e,b_\varphi))\bigr),\quad \text{by~} (x,b_\varphi)=(x,0)(e,b_\varphi)\\
  & =h\bigl(p(x,0)p(e,b_\varphi)\bigr)\\
  & =h\bigl(p_0(x)c_\varphi\bigr)\\
   &=h\bigl(a(q(x))c_\varphi\bigr), \quad \text{by~} p_0=a\circ q.\\
\end{align*}
Since $q$ is onto, $\varphi=u_\varphi\circ a$, where $u_\varphi:L\to [0,1]$ defined by
$u_\varphi(t)=h(tc_\varphi)$ is continuous by separate continuity
in $L$. Thus, we have the following diagram:

\[
\xymatrix@R=2em@C=2.5em{
  G_0 \ar[r]^{p_0} \ar[d]_q &L \ar[ddl]^{u_\varphi} \\
  Y_0 \ar[ur]^a \ar[d]_\varphi & \\
  [0,1] &
}
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:initiality-test} makes $a$ an embedding
of $Y_0$ into the first-countable space $L$, a contradiction with $Y_0$ not first countable.

For~\textup{(iii)}, the universal property of $r:H\to Z$ gives
$\bar F\in C(Z,[0,1])$ with $F=\bar F\circ r$. Then we can define a continuous
map $r_0:G_0\to Z$ by $r_0(x)= r(x,0)$. The universal property of $q:G_0\to Y_0$ gives a continuous map $s:Y_0\to Z$ satisfying
\[
                  s(q(x))=r_0(x)
\]
holds for each $x\in G_0$.
Suppose $\bar F=h\circ p$ through a first-countable semitopological
group $L$.
\[
\xymatrix@R=2em@C=2.5em{
  H\ar[r]^{F} \ar[d]_r &[0,1]  \\
  Z \ar[ur]^{\overline{F}} \ar[d]_p & \\
  L \ar[uur]^{h}&
}
\]
Put $a=p\circ s$. For $\varphi \in C(Y_0,[0,1])$, we have $\varphi\circ q\in C(G_0,[0,1])$. Hence, by Lemma \ref{lem:universal-function}(\ref{eq:all-slices}), there
$b_\varphi \in B$ such that $F(x,b_\varphi)=\varphi(q(x))$ holds for each $x\in G_0$, put $c_\varphi=p(r(e,b_\varphi))$. Because $r$ and $p$
are homomorphisms, the same calculation gives
\begin{align*}
 \varphi(q(x))&=F(x,b_\varphi)\\
 &=h(p(r(x,b_\varphi)))\\
 &=h(p(r(x,0)r(e,b_\varphi)))\\
  &=h(p(r(x,0))p(r(e,b_\varphi)))\\
 &=h(p(r_0(x))c_\varphi)\\
 &=h(a(q(x))c_\varphi).\\
\end{align*}
Since $q$ is onto, $\varphi=u_\varphi\circ a$, where $u_\varphi:L\to [0,1]$ defined by
$u_\varphi(t)=h(tc_\varphi)$ is continuous by separate continuity
in $L$. Thus, we have the following diagram:
\[
\xymatrix{
  G_0 \ar[r]^{r_0} \ar[d]_r & Z \ar[d]^p \\
  Y_0 \ar[ur]^s \ar[r]^{a=p\circ s} \ar[d]_\varphi & L \ar[dl]^{u_\varphi} \\
  {[0,1]} &
}
\]

Lemma~\ref{lem:initiality-test} again gives an embedding
of $Y_0$ into $L$, a contradiction with $Y_0$ not first countable.

The final assertions about the operations follow from products and
Lemma~\ref{lem:weak-topology}. For semiregularity, take products
of regular open basic sets in $G_0$ and $B$: such a product is
regular open, since closure and interior commute with nonempty
finite products.
head: environment

label: thm:main-factorization
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main-factorization}
There exist a Hausdorff quasitopological abelian group $H$, which is
second-countable and semiregular, and a function $F\in C(H,[0,1])$
with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item The regular and Tychonoff reflections of $H$ coincide with a
Tychonoff quasitopological abelian group $Z$ having a countable network.
The canonical map $r:H\to Z$ is
bijective;
\item $F$ does not factor through any continuous homomorphism from
$H$ to a regular first-countable semitopological group;
\item The function $\bar F =\bar F\circ r\in C(Z,[0,1])$ does not
factor through any continuous homomorphism to a first-countable
semitopological group.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, $H$ is $(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{SCSG})$-factorizable but not
$(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{FCSG}_r)$-factorizable, whereas neither $\operatorname{Reg}(H)$ nor
$\operatorname{Tych}(H)$ is $(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{FCSG})$-factorizable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $G$ be the quasitopological group of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-example}. There are a
Polish abelian topological group $B=\mathbb{R}^G\times \mathbb{Z}^{G\times \mathbb{N}}$ and $F\in C(H,[0,1])$ provided
by Lemma~\ref{lem:universal-function} for the underlying space of
$G$, where $H=G\times B$. All the asserted separation
and algebraic properties in Theorem \ref{thm:amplification} now follow. Thus (i)-(iii) follow from (i)-(iii) in Theorem \ref{thm:amplification}, respectively.

Every second-countable
semitopological group is $(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{SCSG})$-factorizable, by using its
identity homomorphism for each continuous real-valued function.
The two failures of factorization are witnessed by $F$ and $\bar F$.
head: environment

label: cor:61-65
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{cor:61-65}
Use $H$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:main-factorization}. Questions~\ref{Q1}, \ref{Q2}, \ref{Q3}, and~\ref{Q4} have negative
answers, even with a second-countable Hausdorff semiregular
quasitopological abelian group as the source. In Questions~\ref{Q1}
and~\ref{Q2} both the regular and the Tychonoff reflection can fail
the asserted factorization property. In Question~\ref{Q4} even regular
first-countable targets are insufficient.
head: environment

label: rem:PW-counterexample
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:PW-counterexample}
The group $H$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:main-factorization} also provides counterexamples to the semitopological
and quasitopological assertions in both~\cite[Theorem~4.2]{PW}
and~\cite[Proposition~4.20]{PW}. Indeed, $H$ is second-countable and
quasitopological, yet it fails factorization even through regular
first-countable semitopological groups. The failed identification
in the proof of the former result was explained in
Remark~\ref{rem:semireg-reflection}.
head: environment

label: lem:symmetrization
title: Lemma
body_md:
~{\cite[Lemma~3.1 and
Proposition~3.4]{Tk2026}}\label{lem:symmetrization}
Let $H$ be a semitopological group.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $H^*$ is a quasitopological group, and the identity
$j:H^*\to H$ is a continuous homomorphism.
\item Every continuous homomorphism $p:G\to H$ from a
quasitopological group has a continuous lift
$p^*:G\to H^*$ with the same underlying homomorphism.
\item If a topological property $\mathcal P$ is invariant under
homeomorphisms and preserved by subspaces and finite products,
then $H\in\mathcal P$ implies $H^*\in\mathcal P$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: thm:transfer-symmetry
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:transfer-symmetry}
Let $\mathcal X$ be any class of topological spaces, and let
$\mathcal P$ satisfy Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetrization}\textup{(iii)}.
For every quasitopological group $G$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $G$ is $(\mathcal X,\mathbb{SG}(\mathcal P))$-factorizable;
\item $G$ is $(\mathcal X,\mathbb{QG}(\mathcal P))$-factorizable.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, each individual factorization in~\textup{(i)} can be
converted into one in~\textup{(ii)} without changing the underlying
homomorphism, its kernel, or the underlying map to the target space.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Only \textup{(i)}$\Rightarrow$\textup{(ii)} needs proof. For a
continuous $f:G\to X$, $X\in\mathcal X$, take
$f=h\circ p$ with $p:G\to H$ continuous and onto and
$H\in\mathbb{SG}(\mathcal P)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetrization},
$p^*:G\to H^*$ is continuous and onto and
$H^*\in\mathbb{QG}(\mathcal P)$. Since the identity $j:H^*\to H$ is continuous,
\[
                      f=(h\circ j)\circ p^*
\]
is the required factorization.
\[
\xymatrix{
  & G \ar[r]^f \ar[d]^p \ar[dl]_{p^*} & X \\
  H^* \ar[r]^j & H \ar[ur]_h &
}
\]
head: environment

label: cor:66-67
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First countability and second countability are hereditary and
finitely productive topological properties. Apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer-symmetry}.
head: environment

label: cor:cardinal
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:cardinal}
The same equivalence holds with first or second countability replaced
by any of the following target conditions: metrizability,
$\chi(H)\leq\kappa$, $w(H)\leq\kappa$, or $\operatorname{nw}(H)\leq\kappa$,
where $\kappa$ is an infinite cardinal. A Hausdorff, regular, or
Tychonoff requirement already imposed on the targets can be retained.
These statements hold for arbitrary $\mathcal X$ in place of $\mathbb{R}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Each listed property, and its conjunction with any listed separation
property, satisfies Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetrization}\textup{(iii)}.
head: environment

label: prop:countable-orbits
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:countable-orbits}
Let $H$ be a countable semitopological group and
$\mathcal F\subseteq C(H,\mathbb{R})$ a countable family. There exist a
second-countable Tychonoff semitopological group $L$ and a continuous
surjective homomorphism $p:H\to L$ such that every member of
$\mathcal F$ factors continuously through $p$. If $H$ is
quasitopological, $L$ can be chosen quasitopological.
head: environment

label: ivan
title: Proof
body_md:
For each function $f:H\to \mathbb{R}$ and $a,b\in H$, define
\begin{equation}\label{ivan}
f_{ab}:H\to \mathbb{R}
\end{equation} by $f_{ab}(x)=f(axb)$ for each $x\in H$.
Since $\mathcal F$ and $H$ are countable, we can obtain a countable family
\[
 \mathcal A=\{f_{ab}: f\in\mathcal F,\ a,b\in H\}.
\]
 Since $H$ is semitopological group and $f$ is continuous, this family consists of continuous functions such that the function $u_{ab}$ is contained in $\mathcal A$ for each $u\in \mathcal A$ and each $a,b\in H$, where $u_{ab}:H\to \mathbb{R}$
 is defined by (\ref{ivan}). Define relation on $H$ by $x\sim y$ when
$u(x)=u(y)$ for every $u\in\mathcal A$. Then translation invariance makes this an equivalence relation. Also, this relation is invariant
under both left and right multiplication. Indeed, if $x\sim y$, then $u(x)=u(y)$ holds for each $u\in\mathcal A$. Hence, $u_{ab}(x)=u_{ab}(y)$ holds for each $a,b\in H$, which implies that $u(axb)=u(ayb)$ by (\ref{ivan}), so $axb\sim ayb$. Thus, the equivalence relation class $N$ containing
the identity $e$ is a normal subgroup: if $n,m\sim e$, then
 translating $m\sim e$ by $n$ gives $nm\sim n\sim e$; translating $n\sim e$ by $n^{-1}$ gives
$n^{-1}\sim e$; and translating $n\sim e$ by $a,a^{-1}$ gives $ana^{-1}\sim e$ for each $a\in H$, which implies that $N$ is a normal subgroup.
Also, we can obtain that the equivalence classes are the cosets of $N$.

Let $p:H\to H/N $ be the natural group homomorphism. Then each $u\in\mathcal A$ induces a function $\overline{u}:H/N\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $u=\overline{u}\circ p$, since $u$ is constant on $xN$ for each $x\in H$.
Put $\overline{\mathcal A}=\{\overline u: u\in\mathcal A\}$. Define the map
\[
 \iota:H/N\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{\overline{\mathcal A}}
 \]
 by $\iota(x)=(\overline u(x))_{\overline{u}\in\overline{\mathcal A}}$ for each $x\in H/N$.
Then $ \iota$ is injective. Indeed, if $x_1\neq x_2$ for $x_1,x_2\in H/N$, then there are $h_1,h_2\in H$ such that $x_1=p(h_1), x_2=p(h_2)$ and $h_1\notin h_2N$, which implies that
there is $u\in \mathcal A$ such that $u(h_1)\neq u(h_2)$. Then $\overline{u}(x_1)\neq \overline{u}(x_2)$ by $u=\overline{ u}\circ p$. Hence, $\iota(x_1)\neq \iota(x_2)$. This proves that $ \iota$ is injective. Give $L=H/N$ the topology $\tau_{\overline{\mathcal A}}$ generated
 by $\overline{\mathcal A}$. i.e., the family $\beta=\{\overline{ u}^{-1}(U): \overline {u}\in \overline{\mathcal A}, U \text{~open in ~}\mathbb{R}\}$ is a subbase of the topology $\tau_{\overline{\mathcal A}}$. Then one can easily show that  $\iota:(L, \tau_{\overline{\mathcal A}})\to \mathbb{R}^{\overline{\mathcal A}}$ is a topological embedding. Hence, $(L, \tau_{\overline{\mathcal A}})$ This is a second-countable Tychonoff space.
Also, the algebraic quotient homomorphism $p:H\to (L, \tau_{\overline{\mathcal A}})$ is continuous,
since each coordinate of $\iota\circ p$ belongs to $\mathcal A$.

Next, we shall prove that $(L, \tau_{\overline{\mathcal A}})$ is a semitopological group when so is $H$. For each $a\in L$, denote the right translation on $L$ by $\rho_a$. Take $x\in H$ such that $a=p(x)$ and denote the right translation on $H$ by $\rho_x$. Take any element $\bar u^{-1}(U)$ of the subbase $\beta$ of the topology $\tau_{\overline{\mathcal A}}$. Then, by the following commutative diagram,
\[
\xymatrix{
H \ar[r]^{\rho_x} \ar[d]^p & H \ar[r]^{u} \ar[d]^p & \mathbb{R} \\
L \ar[r]^{\rho_a} & L \ar[ru]_{\overline {u}} &
}
\]
For any subbase element \(\overline{u}^{-1}(U)\), we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \rho_a^{-1}(\bar u^{-1}(U))&=p(\rho_x^{-1}(u^{-1}(U)))\\
 &=p((u\circ \rho_x)^{-1}(U))\\
  &=p(u_{ex}^{-1}(U)) \qquad \text{by~} u_{ex}=\overline{u_{ex}}\circ p\\
  &=\overline{u_{ex}}^{-1}(U)\in \beta  \qquad \text{by~} \overline{u_{ex}}\in \overline{\mathcal A},
\end{align*}
which implies that $\rho_a:(L,\tau_{\bar{\mathcal A}})\to (L,\tau_{\bar{\mathcal A}})$ is continuous for each $a\in L$. Similarly, using $u_{xe}$ we can show that every left translation on $L$ is continuous. Thus, $(L,\tau_{\bar{\mathcal A}})$ is a semitopological group.

If $H$ is quasitopological, replace $L$ by $L^*$ and use
Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetrization}; the target remains second-countable
and Tychonoff.
head: environment

label: cor:countable
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{cor:countable}
Every countable semitopological group is
$(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{SCSG}_t)$-factorizable. Every countable quasitopological group
is $(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{SCQG}_t)$-factorizable. The same assertions hold for
continuous maps to arbitrary separable metrizable spaces.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a single real-valued function use
Proposition~\ref{prop:countable-orbits}. For a continuous map
$f:H\to X$ with $X$ separable metrizable, embed $X$ into
$\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}$ and apply the proposition simultaneously to its coordinate
functions. The induced map on the common homomorphic image is
continuous into $\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}$ and takes values in the embedded copy of
$X$, as the homomorphism is onto.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let the quasitopological group $G$ be defined by (\ref{eq:cones2}). Then $G$, $\operatorname{Reg}(G)$, and $\operatorname{Tych}(G)$ are all
$(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{SCQG}_t)$-factorizable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Both $G$ and its common reflection $Y$ are countable
quasitopological groups, so it follows from Theorem~\ref{cor:countable}.
head: environment
